subject: octopus
pitch: A curious reef octopus in coral and rust tones, covered in little bumps and paler mottling. A soft, bulbous head, golden eyes with bar-shaped pupils and a slightly grumpy brow. Its eight arms curl out in every direction, each lined with rows of cream suckers, and one arm proudly holds up an old brass key it found on a shipwreck.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module built with the SDK to model an octopus, working out realistic proportions like body height and arm span, with the creature resting with its arms curled on the floor.

For the skeleton, I'm setting up a root body joint with eight tentacle chains radiating from the base of the mantle, curving outward. For the head I'm using a scaled sphere, with golden eyes featuring bar-shaped pupils and a grumpy angled brow above them, plus cream-colored suckers placed along the underside of each arm using along-chain positioning.

I'm working out which direction the sucker-facing normal should point along each chain frame so the suckers consistently sit on one side of the arm, deciding to use the transported normal vector and offset the sucker position outward from the arm's surface along that direction.

Simplifying to a ring of 3 points at 120° spacing and keeping only those with outward.y below zero gives the lower-half placement I want, letting each sucker face outward from the surface and sit flush at the chain point's radius.

Now I'm working through part weighting: I want each sucker rigidly attached to the chain point's joint rather than snapped to the nearest one, so I should pass the bone reference directly, coercing the nullable joint type as needed.

Actually, simplifying by passing `frame: item` along with the outward direction handles both weighting and placement correctly, since the part's `at` defaults to the frame's position. I'm also checking sucker size and embedding depth against the arm radius, then moving on to how each arm chain should curl.

For the arms, I'll build each as a chain along a spiral or catmull path with "tentacle" role, then taper them using a sweep with a radius function that shrinks toward the tip. I'm considering adding surface texture via paint functions like mottle and spots for the coral coloring, and thinking about whether warty bumps should be separate small sphere parts scattered across the head rather than part of the paint itself.

For the bulbous head, I'll make a sphere and scatter dozens of small bump spheres across its surface using a seeded random generator, sticking each one at a scatter hit point with partial embedding. For the eye, I'm placing a golden sphere part and adding a thin dark box as the pupil positioned at the front surface, deciding between literal position offsets and attaching via a hit point for proper placement.

For the brow, I'm using capsules strung between two angled points attached to the head bone to give a grumpy downward slope, passing color through the sweep options since capsule relies on that for its fill. I'm also considering whether the main body should be built from a lathe shape or a simple sphere part to represent the bulbous mantle.

Working out the body geometry now — the mantle is a scaled sphere positioned above the floor, with arm base joints set inside it so the tentacles spiral outward and curl along the ground, tapering in radius from base to tip while keeping their path points above floor level to avoid clipping.

Generating arm curl coordinates...

Naming the chain joints...

Now I need all arms rooted at a shared mantle joint, so I should create the root joint first near y=0.36 and have the arm bases parent to it since they're spawning around y 0.13-0.16.

For the pose and coloring, I'm keeping arms extended with a natural curl, and I'm settling on a coral/rust mottled palette: warm mottle tones for the body, darker stripes for the arms, cream suckers, coral bumps, gold eyes with dark pupils, a brass key accent, and reddish brows. I'll apply paint fills to the sweeps and mantle sphere, making sure the surface data gets properly attached for baking.

Now I'm focusing on the key detail: one arm needs to rise up proudly holding an old brass key. I'm designating arm index 2 as the "raised" arm, giving it a custom curve that lifts higher through its back half before curling at the tip to cradle the key, which I'm building from a torus bow, a shaft, and teeth, oriented vertically so the tentacle tip wraps around the bow. I still need to work out the exact base angle and tip position for this raised arm so the key sits correctly in its grip.

Adding key teeth details and finalizing part placement using default bone attachment, then setting up the tentacle sweep with a tapering radius function and planning sucker placement along each arm using sampled points.

I'm worried about mesh/part count limits if I place suckers at every ring position across all arms, so I'm cutting back the sampling density—reducing to about 9 rows per arm with 2 suckers each to stay under the part and triangle budget.

I should reuse a single small cylinder geometry across all sucker meshes instead of creating one per instance, since three.js allows sharing geometry objects across meshes. I'm also setting their color to a cream tone and aligning each cylinder's axis to the ring's outward direction so they point away from the arm surface correctly.

For the surface bumps, I'm scattering spheres across the mantle using a surface scatter function with minimum distance and a seeded RNG, then sticking small embedded sphere geometries at each hit point, colored brownish-red. Totaling things up: around 144 suckers, roughly 50 bumps, 8 arms, a handful of eye and key parts, plus the mantle itself gives roughly 220 parts overall, which seems manageable. I'm also confirming that the surface scatter function accepts a Part directly since the Part type gets converted into its underlying mesh for the surface target.

Now I'm working out the exact placement for the eyes on the front of the mantle, treating the mantle as an ellipsoid and solving for the surface point at a given x-offset to find where the eye socket should sit, then nudging the eye sphere slightly outward from that point so it bulges convincingly. I'm positioning the eyes symmetrically on either side near the front-top of the head and starting to figure out the grumpy brow shape as a tilted capsule sitting above each eye.

Working out brow capsule endpoints and bone binding...

Now I'm placing eye spheres and pupil boxes, computing exact coordinates so the pupils sit just at the eye surface without clipping. For the arms, I'm setting up an angular distribution around the mantle for seven resting arms plus one raised arm with explicit waypoints defining its curved pose.

Working out where the raised arm's tip should curl near the key bow, accepting a bit of visual overlap as a "wrapping" effect since getting pixel-perfect intersection isn't critical here. I'm ready to start writing the actual geometry code now.

For the other seven arms, I'm designing a procedural curl function: each arm sweeps outward then curls inward in radius while dropping in height toward the tip, so the arms look like they spiral and taper naturally rather than being straight spokes.

Now I'm tuning the base radius formula so the arms attach smoothly where the mantle narrows near the bottom, adjusting coefficients so the tube width at the base matches the mantle's cross-section instead of poking outside it—then chaining each arm's root to the mantle as its parent object.

For coloring, I'm defining a mottled coral-to-cream base skin and layering a countershade effect on top so the arms show a darker coral back fading to a pale underside near the suckers, which should read as more biologically convincing. I'm now writing the sweep call for each arm, passing in the tapering radius function and this composite paint as the color.

Setting up the chain builder using a centripetal Catmull-Rom path through the arm's control points, letting the joint count derive naturally from the number of path spans, and naming each joint programmatically per arm segment with a tentacle role so the rig recognizes it correctly. Then I'm defining the root mantle joint as the base of the hierarchy before attaching parent joints for the arms.

For the suckers, I'm placing rings along each arm's path using the tangent direction as the ring's axis and projecting a flattened world-up vector to establish the outward angle basis -- but I realize this breaks down near-vertical tangent sections where the flattened up vector collapses to zero, falling back to a Z-axis reference that can misplace the 120°/240° outward sucker positions on steeply rising parts of the arm near its base.

I'm working out the filter threshold so suckers land on the lower flanks rather than the top, placing them slightly embedded into the arm's surface at each sampled t along a linspace of nine points, and defining a shared radius-taper function so the sucker rings and the arm's sweep geometry stay consistent.

For the raised key-holding arm, I'm laying out its path points from base to tip, then positioning the key itself above the tip with a vertical shaft, a torus bow at top, and small teeth boxes near the bottom so the arm appears to be gripping it.

I'm reconsidering overall proportions — the model's roughly 0.9m tall with the key at the top, which feels a bit large for a stylized reef octopus but should read fine visually given the arm span. Now I'm working out the mantle sphere's placement and scale with eyes positioned on it, and thinking through how the paint/chartify texturing will interact with that non-uniform scaling.

I'll keep the bumps confined to the mantle rather than extending them onto the arms.

The sucker centre sits at 0.96r radially with the ring's three items placed at 0°, 120°, and 240°, and since for horizontal arms the vertical component works out so the 120° and 240° points land below the line, filtering by outward.y < 0 correctly picks the lower two suckers while excluding the top one. With arms covering nine rows along the body and the ring/sweep radius functions matching, the module structure takes shape: a default export function building the octopus with a reef-octopus builder, pulling in createBuilder, catmull, countershade, mottle, and rng from the builder library. Since paint objects aren't functions, passing a Paint instance as a color function safely falls through to null, so colorAt still resolves correctly using the band-less path.

Nesting countershade over a mottle-generated coral color works fine since Paint is an accepted color input, and I'll keep bump painting, brow strings, and bar-shaped pupils as already planned, skipping extra arm spots for now. I'm defining the raised-arm chain with explicit catmull points and starting to write the actual export code.
